text: Every dataset should already be governed under an existing data governance program, classified, owned, access-controlled. Training data needs something more, because of what happens to it once it's used.

A report built on bad data gets corrected when someone catches the mistake and rebuilds it. A model trained on bad data keeps producing the consequences of that mistake until someone retrains it, and retraining is slower and more expensive than editing a report.

A serious training data policy answers, before any model gets trained: where is this data allowed to come from, internal systems, licensed data, public datasets, web-scraped data each carry different risk. Who approved its use for this purpose, repurposing data collected for one reason to train a model is a different decision than using it for its original purpose. What's the quality bar before training starts.
Does it reflect the population the model will actually be used on, a mismatch here is one of the main ways bias enters a model. How was it labeled, and by whom, labeling is its own governed activity.

Once a model finishes training, the data points it learned from aren't in a queryable table anymore, they're compressed into statistical patterns across the model's parameters. That makes it much harder to later remove the influence of one bad data point, you often have to retrain from scratch, not delete a row, and much harder to prove exactly what the model did or didn't learn from a source.
That's why training data decisions get reviewed before training, not just audited after. Next up: data provenance and consent, where the data actually came from and whether its use was allowed.
